stem: A 38-year-old man has sudden severe colicky right flank pain spreading to the groin, with vomiting. Urine microscopy shows red cells and no casts. A noncontrast CT shows a 5-mm stone with dilation of the ureter above it. On the scout film the stone projects over the upper part of the right sacroiliac joint.
oneliner: 38M + colicky right flank pain to groin + vomiting + hematuria, no casts + 5-mm ureteral stone over the upper sacroiliac joint → ?
ask: At which normal narrowing of the ureter has the stone most likely lodged?

options.A: Where the gonadal vessels cross in front of it at L3
options.B: Where it lies on the psoas at mid-abdomen
options.C: Where it crosses the iliac vessels at the pelvic brim
options.D: Beside the lower pole of the kidney
options.E: Where the ductus deferens crosses above it

whyNot.A: The gonadal vessels simply cross **in front of** the ureter at about **L3** without narrowing it; this stone lies lower, **over the sacroiliac joint**
whyNot.B: The ureter runs smoothly over psoas in the **mid-abdomen**; this stone sits lower, **over the sacroiliac joint**
whyNot.D: The ureter has not narrowed yet beside the kidney; the stone is **down at the sacroiliac joint**, not at the lower renal pole
whyNot.E: The vas crosses the ureter **deep in the pelvis** just before the bladder; this stone is higher, **over the upper sacroiliac joint**

answer: Where it crosses the iliac vessels at the pelvic brim
why: The ureter narrows at three sites: the **ureteropelvic junction**, the **pelvic brim where it crosses the iliac vessels**, and the **ureterovesical junction**, the narrowest. A stone projecting **over the upper sacroiliac joint** is at the brim, where the ureter crosses the common iliac bifurcation.

idea.rule: Stones lodge at the three ureteral narrowings: ureteropelvic junction, pelvic brim and ureterovesical junction.
also: The ureteropelvic junction is where the renal pelvis tapers into the ureter
The ureterovesical junction, where the ureter enters the bladder wall, is the narrowest point
At the pelvic brim the ureter passes over the bifurcation of the common iliac artery
Hydroureter above the stone and hydronephrosis follow obstruction at any of these sites

stem: A 63-year-old woman has had fever and right flank pain for 4 days. She had an obstructing ureteric stone treated 3 weeks ago. Her temperature is 38.6 C. CT shows a fluid collection in the fat on the posteromedial side of the right kidney.
oneliner: 63F + fever + right flank pain + recent ureteric stone + collection posteromedial to the right kidney → ?
ask: Along which fascia is the infection most likely to extend downward?

whyNot.B: Lies behind the **lateral** part of the kidney; this collection is **posteromedial**
whyNot.C: Forms the **lateral abdominal wall** beyond quadratus lumborum, away from a **posteromedial** collection
whyNot.D: A **superficial back muscle**, separated from the kidney by deeper muscles; a posteromedial perirenal collection does not reach it
whyNot.E: Part of the **anterolateral** abdominal wall, far from the **posteromedial** surface of the kidney

why: The kidney rests **medially on psoas major** and laterally on quadratus lumborum and transversus abdominis. A collection on the **posteromedial** kidney therefore tracks down along the **psoas fascia**.

idea.rule: The kidney lies on psoas, quadratus lumborum and transversus abdominis, so posteromedial pus follows psoas.
also: A psoas abscess gives pain on hip extension (psoas sign)
Perinephric abscess often follows pyelonephritis or an obstructing stone
Pus along psoas can reach the femoral triangle and upper thigh
Tuberculosis of the spine (Pott disease) can also track along psoas

stem: A 58-year-old man leaks urine whenever he stands or coughs, starting right after a radical prostatectomy. The surgeon reports damage to the nerve plexus beside the prostate that supplies the sphincter at the bladder neck. He can still stop his urine stream voluntarily, and perineal sensation is normal.
oneliner: 58M + leaks urine on standing or coughing since radical prostatectomy + injured nerve plexus to bladder-neck sphincter + can still stop stream voluntarily → ?
ask: Which tissue type has lost its function?

whyNot.A: Skeletal muscle forms the **external sphincter** under the pudendal nerve; he **can still stop his stream voluntarily**
whyNot.B: A **lining** epithelium; denervation cannot impair a tissue that does not contract
whyNot.D: Found in tendons and ligaments, with **no contractile or nerve-driven function**
whyNot.E: Found in capsules and dermis, with **no contractile or nerve-driven function**

why: The **internal urethral sphincter** at the bladder neck is **smooth muscle** under **sympathetic (alpha-1)** control, and its nerves run beside the prostate. The **external sphincter** is skeletal muscle supplied by the **pudendal nerve**, which still works here.

idea.rule: Internal sphincter is involuntary smooth muscle; external sphincter is voluntary skeletal muscle on the pudendal nerve.
also: Sympathetic fibers close the internal sphincter during ejaculation to prevent retrograde flow
Alpha-1 blockers such as tamsulosin relax the bladder neck in BPH
The detrusor is smooth muscle contracted by parasympathetic M3 receptors
The external sphincter lies in the deep perineal pouch

stem: A 31-year-old man is brought in after a motorcycle crash with a fractured pelvis. There is blood at the urethral meatus, he cannot pass urine despite a full bladder, and on rectal examination the prostate is felt higher than normal. A retrograde urethrogram is planned.
oneliner: 31M + motorcycle crash + pelvic fracture + blood at meatus + cannot void with full bladder + high-riding prostate → ?
ask: Which part of the urethra is most likely torn?

whyNot.A: Torn by a **straddle injury** or a traumatic catheter; this man's injury is a **pelvic fracture**
whyNot.B: Injured by **direct penile trauma** or instruments; the problem here is **pelvic**, with a **high-riding prostate**
whyNot.C: Lies inside the prostate and is hurt by **instrumentation**; the **prostate is displaced upward**, so the tear is below the gland
whyNot.D: The **distal** dilation inside the glans, far from the pelvis, and a **high-riding prostate** points proximally

why: A **pelvic fracture** tears the **membranous urethra** where it is fixed in the urogenital diaphragm. The prostate is then displaced upward (**high-riding**) and blood appears at the **meatus**.

idea.rule: Pelvic fracture tears the membranous (posterior) urethra; a straddle injury tears the bulbar (anterior) urethra.
also: A straddle injury causes a bulbar urethral tear with a butterfly perineal hematoma
Retrograde urethrography comes before any catheter when urethral injury is suspected
Pelvic fracture can also rupture the bladder
The membranous urethra is the shortest and least distensible part of the male urethra

stem: A 2-week-old boy with severe dehydration after gastroenteritis develops thrombosis of both renal veins. The right kidney infarcts, but the left kidney is spared.
oneliner: 2-week-old M + dehydration + bilateral renal vein thrombosis + right kidney infarcts, left kidney spared → ?
ask: Collateral drainage through which vein most likely spared the left kidney?

whyNot.A: Drains **straight into the IVC** below the renal vein and offers the right kidney **no collateral**, which is why it infarcted
whyNot.C: Drains into the portal system and has **no normal connection** to the left renal vein
whyNot.D: Drains the gut into the portal vein; it does **not normally communicate** with the left kidney
whyNot.E: Drains the left colon and rectum toward the portal system; it **does not feed the left renal vein**

why: The **left renal vein** receives the **left gonadal and left suprarenal veins**, which provide collateral outflow when it clots. The short **right renal vein** enters the IVC directly with no such tributaries, so the right kidney infarcts.

idea.rule: The left gonadal and suprarenal veins drain into the left renal vein, whereas the right ones drain straight into the IVC.
also: The right gonadal vein enters the IVC directly
The left renal vein passes between the SMA and the aorta
Nutcracker syndrome compresses the left renal vein and can cause a left varicocele
Renal vein thrombosis is also seen in nephrotic syndrome, especially membranous

stem: A 44-year-old woman starts a trek at 3,500 m and takes a tablet to prevent mountain sickness. Her urine becomes alkaline and rich in bicarbonate. Blood tests show a mild hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis with a normal anion gap.
oneliner: 44F + high-altitude trek + tablet for mountain sickness + alkaline bicarbonate-rich urine + hyperchloremic normal-anion-gap acidosis → ?
ask: At which nephron segment does this drug mainly act?

options.B: Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle
options.E: Thin descending limb of the loop of Henle

whyNot.B: Loop diuretics act here and cause **metabolic alkalosis**, not a hyperchloremic acidosis with **bicarbonate-rich urine**
whyNot.C: Thiazides act here and also tend to cause **metabolic alkalosis**; they do not make the urine **rich in bicarbonate**
whyNot.D: Potassium-sparing diuretics act here; any acidosis they cause comes with **little bicarbonate in the urine**, and they do not prevent mountain sickness
whyNot.E: Permeable to water but with **no diuretic target**; **bicarbonate is not reabsorbed here**

why: This is **acetazolamide**, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor acting in the **proximal convoluted tubule**. Filtered **bicarbonate is not reabsorbed**, so the urine turns alkaline and a **non-anion-gap acidosis** results, which drives breathing at altitude.

idea.rule: The proximal tubule reabsorbs bicarbonate, so carbonic anhydrase inhibitors waste it.
also: Alkaline urine promotes calcium phosphate stones
Acetazolamide is also used for glaucoma and idiopathic intracranial hypertension
Paresthesias and sulfa-allergy cross-reaction are known adverse effects
Most filtered bicarbonate is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule
